alternatives: Rivastigmine transdermal patch 4.6 mg/24 h: transdermal delivery may reduce gastrointestinal effects; not metabolised by CYP enzymes.
Galantamine ER 8 mg daily: alternative cholinesterase inhibitor.
interactions: Donepezil + Atorvastatin: no clinically significant interaction; both are CYP3A4 substrates without mutual inhibition at standard doses.
Donepezil + Aspirin: cholinesterase inhibitors increase gastric acid secretion; with aspirin, monitor for dyspepsia and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Donepezil + Amlodipine: no clinically significant interaction; amlodipine does not slow the heart rate.
Donepezil + Losartan, Metformin, Glipizide, Alendronate: no clinically significant interaction.
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope can occur; baseline pulse 72 bpm and no rate-slowing medicine on the list. Check pulse at each dose increase; caution with sick sinus syndrome or other conduction disorder.
Nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss are common at initiation; start at 5 mg at night and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated.
No dose adjustment for renal impairment (eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73 m2).
Anticholinergic medicines oppose the effect of cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid combining.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 22/30 and MoCA 18/30 with recall not improved by cues, son-confirmed decline over eighteen months, and loss of instrumental independence (supervised medicines, stove guards, driving stopped), staging the syndrome as mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: She lives alone and her son has taken over parts of her medicines and kitchen safety, so an explicit functional account with a validated instrument stages the syndrome as dementia [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe amnestic multi-domain profile: verbal and visual delayed recall below the 1st percentile with impaired recognition, plus naming, semantic fluency and set-shifting deficits
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile, quantify severity, and establish baseline
action_criteria.rationale: A storage-type amnestic profile points to Alzheimer pathology rather than the dysexecutive, retrieval-type pattern expected if her severe small vessel disease were the main cause [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, B12, folate and RPR normal; HbA1c 7.8%, LDL 104 mg/dL, triglycerides 178 mg/dL and eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73m2 identify modifiable vascular and metabolic contributors
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Reversible causes must be excluded, and her diabetes, dyslipidaemia and kidney disease quantified, because they drive the small vessel disease that contributes to her decline [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral MTA grade 2-3 with temporoparietal and precuneus atrophy, together with Fazekas 3 white matter disease, multiple lacunes and microbleeds: dual pathology
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to characterize medial temporal atrophy and assess cerebrovascular burden
action_criteria.rationale: MRI weighs the neurodegenerative pattern (medial temporal and precuneus atrophy) against the vascular burden expected after a prior stroke and decades of hypertension [NIA_AA_2011] [STRIVE_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity with tau pathology: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio (0.046) with elevated p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Donepezil can be started: no significant interaction with her medicines, no renal dose change, gastrointestinal bleeding caution with aspirin, pulse check for bradycardia
action_criteria.label: After the diagnosis is staged and disclosed, check donepezil against her current medicines and kidney function before starting it
action_criteria.rationale: A post-diagnostic safety step: she takes seven medicines and has stage G3a kidney disease, so the cholinesterase inhibitor that the mild dementia stage supports is checked before it is prescribed [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose pure vascular cognitive impairment on the basis of Fazekas 3 white matter disease and lacunes alone; the storage-type amnestic profile and medial temporal atrophy indicate Alzheimer disease with vascular copathology.
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97].
required_recommendations: Disclose mild Alzheimer dementia with contributory small vessel disease to the patient and her son, and discuss prognosis, advance directives, durable power of attorney for health and finances, and community support [NIA_AA_2011].

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines (pulse 72 bpm, no rate-slowing medicine), with doses supervised through the lockbox dispenser [NICE_NG97].

Manage the vascular contributors: blood pressure toward below 130/80 mmHg if tolerated without orthostatic symptoms (148/88 in clinic, home readings above 170/100), intensify lipid lowering for LDL 104 mg/dL toward below 70 mg/dL after her stroke, and keep aspirin for secondary prevention [AHA_secondary_stroke_2021].

Review her diabetes treatment for hypoglycaemia risk: glipizide in a woman with dementia who lives alone and cannot recall whether she took her medicines; HbA1c 7.8% is close to the individualised target of below 8.0% for older adults with cognitive impairment, so avoid intensification that risks hypoglycaemia and consider replacing the sulfonylurea; keep metformin within the dose for eGFR 44 [ADA_older_adults_2026].

Address safety for a woman living alone: confirm she does not resume driving, keep medicines supervised and the stove guarded, transfer bill payment to her son or automatic payments, and assess the need for home support or a change in living arrangement [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in AD and not part of routine dementia workup; no seizure concern or encephalopathy to justify it
ECG is unrelated to the dementia diagnostic workup; no cardiac symptom, syncope, or arrhythmia indication
Echocardiography is not indicated in the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication (no AF, no structural lesion) in this case despite vascular risk factors
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no palpitations, syncope, or arrhythmia in this presentation
Head CT is inferior to MRI for dementia workup; MRI was already obtained and is the preferred structural modality
DaTscan is indicated for suspected parkinsonism or DLB differentiation; no core DLB features (no visual hallucinations, no significant parkinsonism, no REM sleep behavior disorder) are present

accepted: Early-stage Alzheimer's disease (mild dementia, amnestic) with cerebral small-vessel disease (contributory)

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment (contributory small vessel disease)
differential.key_features: A real contributor rather than the primary cause: Fazekas 3 white matter disease, multiple lacunes, microbleeds, a prior stroke and long-standing vascular risk factors; the storage-type amnestic profile with no benefit from cues, MTA grade 2-3 with precuneus atrophy, and a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 with raised p-tau when tested are not features of pure vascular cognitive impairment

A plausible framing when vascular burden is severe; the amnestic profile and medial temporal and precuneus atrophy (and the Alzheimer CSF pattern when tested) indicate that Alzheimer pathology is the dominant process
No visual hallucinations, no fluctuations, no REM sleep behavior disorder; mild bilateral rigidity without bradykinesia or tremor does not meet parkinsonism

GDS 6/15 is borderline and she feels sad at times, but she denies sustained low mood or anhedonia, and the storage-type memory deficit with impaired recognition and medial temporal atrophy argue against depression as the primary cause
No early personality change, disinhibition or hyperorality; memory is the dominant deficit, and frontal release signs occur in Alzheimer dementia

key_clinical_evidence: Fazekas grade 3 white matter disease with a dense vascular risk profile anchors toward pure vascular cognitive impairment, but a storage-type amnestic deficit with impaired recognition is not the dysexecutive pattern of small vessel disease [STRIVE_2013].

MTA grade 2-3 with temporoparietal and precuneus atrophy is a neurodegeneration marker that supports Alzheimer disease as the primary process even when vascular disease is severe; when amyloid status is tested, a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 with raised p-tau confirms it [NIA_AA_2018].

Vascular copathology is contributory and modifiable: blood pressure and lipid control after stroke, and a diabetes regimen that avoids hypoglycaemia in an older adult with dementia, are part of the management.
Frontal release signs (palmomental, snout, glabellar) are common in Alzheimer dementia and do not suggest frontotemporal dementia without an early behavioural or language presentation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas 3 white matter disease and lacunes establish significant small vessel disease as a contributor, but do not override Alzheimer disease as the primary process: the storage-type amnestic profile and MTA grade 2-3 atrophy point to Alzheimer disease with vascular copathology
red_herrings.data_point: Fazekas grade 3 periventricular and subcortical white matter hyperintensities with multiple lacunar infarcts and microhemorrhages on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on cerebral small vessel disease as the primary diagnosis (vascular cognitive impairment) and defer or omit AD biomarker workup on the assumption that the white matter burden explains all cognitive deficits

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior stroke and vascular risk factors explain part of the white matter burden, but a remote, fully recovered posterior circulation stroke cannot explain a progressive amnestic multi-domain dementia with bilateral medial temporal atrophy twelve years later; a neurodegenerative process must be sought
red_herrings.data_point: History of ischemic stroke 12 years ago with complete recovery, plus hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia: a dense vascular risk factor profile
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat the cognitive syndrome as a sequela of cerebrovascular disease and historical stroke rather than a neurodegenerative process

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect; particularly important in this older patient with significant vascular burden and microhemorrhages on MRI
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.
The cholinesterase-inhibitor safety check follows the staging of the syndrome as dementia.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Amyloid status optional, by CSF or amyloid PET (one conclusive test); the donepezil safety check is an optional post-diagnostic step.
key_educational_points: Fazekas grade 3 white matter hyperintensities in a patient with longstanding vascular risk factors create a strong anchoring trap toward pure vascular cognitive impairment; the storage-type amnestic profile and medial temporal atrophy point to Alzheimer disease, and amyloid biomarkers help when uncertainty remains

The neuropsychological signature of AD (amnestic-predominant, storage-type deficit, no recognition benefit) differs from that of VCI (subcortical/frontal, retrieval-type deficit, benefit from cues); this distinction is clinically important even when both pathologies coexist
The NIA-AA 2018 framework applies to individuals with concurrent vascular pathology: an Alzheimer biomarker profile identifies Alzheimer disease regardless of comorbid white matter disease
Vascular copathology is contributory and modifiable; aggressive management of blood pressure, glycemia, and lipids is a critical action alongside AD-specific workup and treatment
In the oldest-old (age 75+), mixed pathology dementia is the rule rather than the exception; a single unifying diagnosis rarely accounts for the full cognitive picture
Amyloid status can be established by CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET; one conclusive test is enough

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Eleanor Hartley is a 79-year-old right-handed retired bank manager who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her son, Richard, for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline. Richard first noticed changes approximately 18 months ago when his mother, who had always been meticulously organized and financially astute, began missing scheduled bill payments and later discovered she had paid the same electric bill twice in one month. At the time he attributed this to the stress of living alone, but over the following months more concerning changes emerged. She began calling him multiple times in a single day asking the same questions, apparently unaware she had called earlier. She forgot about a granddaughter's birthday dinner she had agreed to attend and was visibly confused when the family arrived at her door. More recently, she has been unable to recall recent news events she had watched on television the same day and cannot remember whether she has taken her morning medications, prompting Richard to purchase a lockbox pill dispenser. Her word-finding difficulties have worsened; she now pauses frequently mid-sentence and substitutes descriptive phrases for words she cannot retrieve. She has not driven for approximately three months after she became lost in the neighborhood adjacent to her own condominium complex, a route she has traveled for over fifteen years. She continues to manage basic self-care independently (dressing, bathing, and preparing simple meals), though Richard reports she has twice left a pot on the stove and forgotten it, prompting him to install stove-knob guards. She denies hallucinations. Her son confirms there have been no episodes of seeing things that are not present, no marked fluctuations in alertness, and no dream-enactment behaviors at night. Personality has changed subtly; she is less interested in her grandchildren and in the crossword puzzles she previously completed daily, but there is no disinhibition, compulsive behavior, or hypersexuality. She reports feeling sad at times about her declining memory but denies a sustained low mood, anhedonia, or suicidal ideation. She was evaluated by her primary care physician nine months ago who ordered basic metabolic labs and a brain CT; she recalls being told the CT showed 'some white matter changes consistent with her history' but does not recall the details. She was referred for neurology evaluation at that time but the appointment was delayed. Her vascular risk factors, particularly her blood pressure, have been incompletely controlled over the past several years; her son notes her home blood pressure readings have sometimes exceeded 170/100 mmHg and her physician recently increased her antihypertensive regimen.
